# The signed-PDF corpus

Generated by `research/tools/gen_pades_corpus.py`, which signs a page with
pyHanko and records what pyHanko reports about the result. Both `pdfa` and
`pades` test against these same documents, so the reader and the verifier cannot
drift apart.

| file | what it is | what a verifier must say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `blank.pdf` | one page, no signature | no signature at all |
| `signed_bb.pdf` | signed once, nothing appended | intact, covers the whole file, B-B |
| `signed_lt.pdf` | signed, then validation data appended | intact, covers its revision, B-LT |
| `appended.pdf` | a byte appended after the signed range | intact, covers its revision |
| `tampered.pdf` | a byte flipped inside the signed range | broken |

`signed_lt.pdf` is the case worth understanding: the DSS is appended *after*
signing on purpose, so the signature covers a revision and not the file. A
verifier that demands the whole file be covered rejects every long-term-valid
document, which is why `pades::Coverage` has three cases rather than a boolean.

`appended.pdf` is the mirror image and equally important: appending a byte does
not break integrity, because the appended byte is outside the signed range. So
"something follows the signature" is not evidence of tampering.

`signed_lt_contents.hex` is the `/Contents` of `signed_lt.pdf`, and
`signed_lt_cert.der` is the certificate inside it, extracted so the CMS and
X.509 readers can be tested without going through the PDF.

The files are regenerated with a fresh key each time, so the bytes are not
stable. Tests assert on the pyHanko labels, never on a byte offset, so a
regenerated corpus keeps passing.
